The object of a word, which acts to produce cognition, 
is in no way external. 
Because there is no other entity, and it is not an actual thing, 
if one proves that this very intention to speak 
is what makes something understood, 
it is completely clear as the third characteristic.

If the intention to speak has not become manifest, 
one does not employ speech. 
A butter lamp itself is not an instrument of cognition 
toward blue and the like purely by virtue of being an inferential sign <note>Tibetan: <term>rtags</term>, Sanskrit: <term>liṅga</term></note>. 
Because it is capable of generating cognition 
upon its arising, it is spoken of in that way. 
If it is the actuality of an inferential sign that causes cognition, 
consider the property of the subject <note>Tibetan: <term>phyogs kyi chos</term>, Sanskrit: <term>pakṣadharma</term></note> and the rest! 
Why would one not debate 
in terms of "otherwise impossible" <note>Tibetan: <term>gzhan du mi 'thad pa</term>, Sanskrit: <term>anyathānupapatti</term></note> and the like? 
Why not establish being apprehended by the eye 
as being simply impossible otherwise? 

Because it lacks the property of the subject, 
the position asserting only one characteristic is deficient. 
Those who state only one form 
actually demonstrate the second form. 
By stating the two forms, 
the three forms follow from the property of the subject. 
If one objects that it is implied 
by being impossible otherwise, that is not so; 
otherwise, one would have to accept that sounds and the like 
are apprehended by the eye!

Because an argument such as "being his son" 
is not contradictory to the dissimilar class, 
its negative concomitance <note>Tibetan: <term>ldog pa</term>, Sanskrit: <term>vyatireka</term></note> is doubtful; 
therefore, the three forms are not present. 
Even though he is the son of that son, 
due to the variation of causes 
such as karma and diet, 
entities invariably turn into something else. 
This is neither an effect, an essential nature, 
nor a non-perception of the visible. 
If it is not different from that, 
it becomes infallible. 

If such infallibility 
were also seen in other cases: 
for example, the rising of the moon is the sign 
for the blooming of the water-lily <note>Sanskrit: <term>kumuda</term></note> and the swelling of the ocean; 
from seeing something blazing, 
one knows thoroughly that shade exists 
in other parts; 
seeing a burning firebrand in the dark, 
one infers smoke from afar; 
and from the rising of the Pleiades <note>Tibetan: <term>smin drug</term>, Sanskrit: <term>kṛttikā</term></note>, 
one realizes that Rohiṇī <note>Tibetan: <term>snar ma</term></note> is near; 
in this case, that property of the reason

<summary>This text critiques single-aspect theories of logical reason in Buddhist epistemology, defending the standard three criteria of a valid sign while analyzing causal and natural relationships across various classical astronomical and natural analogies.</summary>
<keywords>pramana, trirupa, pakṣadharma, vyatireka, anyathanupapatti, inference, logic, Buddhist epistemology</keywords>

Fascicle Two.

By stating the property of the subject <term>pakṣadharma</term> <gloss>the presence of the logical reason in the subject</gloss> along with positive and negative concomitance <term>anvayavyatireka</term> <gloss>agreement in presence and absence</gloss>, this explains both ascertained positive and negative concomitance, and it also explains the ascertained property of the subject. Because the means of ascertainment are similar, positive and negative concomitance are explained distinct from the mere property of the subject. 

Here, one should not understand the phrase "both positive and negative concomitance are also explained" in a superficial sense. When the understanding of one thing also leads to the effect of understanding another, it is reasonable to state it in this manner. However, once that which is exclusively stated has already been explained, stating it again in this way would serve no purpose. 

If one asks: "Even if pervasion is realized through that aspect, is it not for the sake of expressing that?" 
It is not so. Through phrases such as "as for pervasion," these are realized according to how its essential nature is stated. What other realization could there be regarding the property of the subject itself, such that one would say: "The property of the subject is also explained"? 

Therefore, even though ascertainment was taught without being explicitly named, the text sets forth the meaning that ascertainment itself is indeed what is expressed. 

If one asks: "What kind of ascertainment is it here?" 
In order to encompass those three modes <note>the three criteria of a valid reason: presence in the subject, positive pervasion, and negative pervasion</note> where that exists, the text says: "Those are..." The property of the subject and that which is pervaded by its aspects constitute the three logical reasons characterized as effect, nature, and non-perception.

When presenting the three aforementioned logical marks with examples, explaining how the three such as the effect are "like this and like that" spans from the phrase "for example" up to the phrase "it is explained." 

Therefore, following the aforementioned sequence, the effect is introduced first, the essential nature is second, and non-perception is last. Setting forth both the logical reason and the probandum <term>sādhya</term> <gloss>that which is to be proved</gloss> serves to demonstrate the essential nature of cause and effect. 

An example of the reason of essential nature <term>svabhāvahetu</term> is: "Because it is a <term>śiṃśapā</term> <gloss>rosewood tree</gloss>." <summary>This text comments on Buddhist logic, detailing the three modes of a valid reason and the requirement of certainty in positive and negative concomitance. It introduces the three classes of valid reasons: effect, essential nature, and non-perception.</summary>
